Dream-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Worlds

Tong Zheng Affiliation: \thepa Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park    Xidong Wu Affiliation: \thepa    Zheng Zhang Affiliation: \thepa    Zhankui He Affiliation: Google Deepmind    Chaoyi Zhang Affiliation: \thepa    Benjamin Coleman Affiliation: Google Deepmind    Ruoqiao Wei Affiliation: \thepa    Di Bai Affiliation: Google Deepmind    Haolin Liu Affiliation: University of Virginia    Rui Liu Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park    Xue Wang Affiliation: \thepa    Yue Zhuan Affiliation: \thepa    Wang-Cheng Kang Affiliation: Google Deepmind    Renkai Xiang Affiliation: \thepa    Heng Huang Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park    Xinwu Cheng Affiliation: \thepa    Yunsong Guo Affiliation: \thepa
Abstract

Recursive self-improvement is becoming essential for autonomous AI agents, whose progress depends on discovering high-value solutions across complex domains. Effective exploration drives this process, yet managing and improving exploration strategies remains a major bottleneck. Current systems face a fundamental dilemma: fixed strategies fail to adapt as search spaces scale, while online policy optimization must navigate vast meta-search spaces under delayed, expensive feedback from long-horizon rollouts. We introduce Dream-RSI, a framework for scalable, recursively self-improving exploration. A lightweight orchestration layer makes exploration explicit and programmable while leaving the underlying base agent unchanged. Our key insight is that accumulated discovery history can act as a replay simulator over the realized search space. By dreaming within this simulator built from historical discovery trees, Dream-RSI obtains immediate, low-cost off-policy feedback to evaluate and refine exploration policies without repeated, expensive online evaluation. The improved policy is then redeployed online to drive further discovery, continuously expanding the simulator pool in a self-improving loop. Across 9 tasks in 4 domains, Dream-RSI achieves competitive quality and improves discovery efficiency in several settings.  github.com/zhengkid/Dream-RSI   |    dream-rsi.com

1 Introduction

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has emerged as an ambitious goal for autonomous AI systems (Liu et al., 2026c). A common mechanism underlying RSI is an iterative loop wherein agents propose candidate solutions, evaluate outcomes, and fold the resulting feedback into subsequent iterations. Such loops have driven substantial progress across algorithm design (Novikov et al., 2025; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), open-ended mathematical optimization (Georgiev et al., 2025; Anthropic, 2026), systems design (Jaber and Jaber, 2026; Cao et al., 2026), and agent self-improvement (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c; Lee et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026a). As agents grow stronger and self-improvement targets grow harder, discovery demands long-horizon exploration over vast search spaces, often spanning thousands of proposal-evaluation cycles (Ye et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2026). At this scale, orchestrating exploration becomes critical (Zheng et al., 2026b): poor exploration wastes computation and time, sharply limiting the efficiency and scalability of RSI.

Existing approaches largely rely on manually designed exploration strategies that stay fixed throughout discovery (Novikov et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026b; Du et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). Such strategies cannot learn from accumulated experience and may repeatedly spend computation on unproductive search directions. Recent work therefore attempts to optimize exploration policies online (Liu et al., 2026a), but this faces two fundamental bottlenecks. First, meta-level feedback is delayed and expensive. Unlike evaluating a single candidate, assessing an exploration policy requires observing how it shapes discovery over many proposal–evaluation cycles. Second, the meta-policy space is vast, so many alternatives must be tried before a good one is found. Together, these make meta-level improvement costly. Each policy demands a long online rollout before yielding useful signal, making the self-improvement loop hard to close at the exploration layer.

To address these bottlenecks, we want to design a fast and cheap simulator of discovery to prune exploration policies before costly online deployment. Surprisingly, completed discovery histories already provide such a simulator. Prior work treats past history merely as static textual context (Hu et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2026b) or as training data for fine-tuning (Yuksekgonul et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). Yet a completed discovery process inherently records a structured tree of exploration decisions and their realized code-execution outcomes. By analogy to model-based reinforcement learning and World Models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2023) (§2), this discovery history can serve as a replay simulator11 1 We use replay simulator and world interchangeably.. Figure 2 shows an alternative strategy can navigate this pre-recorded tree, traversing different subsets of branches in different orders, with different parallel groupings and stopping decisions. Since all execution results are locally stored, evaluating a new strategy requires only reading past records. This turns meta-policy improvement from expensive online trial-and-error into a fast, simulation-based “dreaming” procedure.

Building on this insight, we introduce Dream-RSI, a framework for scalable, recursively self-improving meta-exploration in agent-driven discovery. We first make exploration programmable through a lightweight orchestration layer that controls branching, parallelism, and stopping while leaving the underlying base agent unchanged. To improve this policy, Dream-RSI follows a self-improvement loop (Figure 1): (1) Online Exploration, where the current policy drives real-world discovery and logs execution traces; (2) Replay Simulator Construction, where recorded discovery trees become a reusable replay simulator pool; and (3) Dreaming-based Policy Improvement, where candidate policies are cheaply evaluated by dreaming over the simulator. The updated policy is redeployed online, generating new experience that expands the simulator pool and closing an RSI loop at the meta-exploration layer. We evaluate Dream-RSI on 9 discovery tasks across four domains. On algorithm engineering (Lasso path solver), it outperforms sklearn and strong baselines while using up to 162×162\times fewer agent calls than SimpleTES. On mathematical optimization, it matches or exceeds the best results among the compared baselines on two of three tasks. On GPU kernel engineering (KernelBench), it reaches similar speeds with 1.79×1.79\times–2.43×2.43\times fewer generations, or improves kernel performance by up to 2.09×2.09\times under a comparable budget. On harness optimization, it improves the seed harness by over 8 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Our contributions are: 1) History as Replay Simulator. We recast completed discovery histories as replay simulators, making delayed exploration feedback reusable for cheap meta-exploration policy evaluation. 2) Meta-Layer RSI Loop. We introduce Dream-RSI, to our knowledge the first framework to close a meta-layer RSI loop using discovery history as a replay simulator. 3) Empirical Validation. Across nine tasks in four domains, Dream-RSI achieves competitive discovery quality and improves discovery-agent-call efficiency in several settings.

2 Motivation: Discovery History as a Replay Simulator

Consider an agent navigating an unfamiliar environment. On its first attempt it wanders, hits dead ends, and backtracks — but in doing so it builds a map. That map is reusable: a new policy can plan over it, skip known dead ends, revisit earlier choices, and compare routes without physically walking them again (Gupta et al., 2017). This is the logic of model-based reinforcement learning (Sutton, 1990; M. Moerland et al., 2023). A model of how the environment responds to actions lets policies be trained or evaluated in simulation instead of through repeated real interaction (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018). The Dreamer family (Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2023; Hafner et al., 2025) is the clearest example: learn a compact dynamics model from collected experience, then improve the policy by imagining trajectories inside it.

Long-horizon discovery has the same structure. An exploration policy decides which directions to pursue, which candidates to refine, what to branch on in parallel, and when to stop. Running it online leaves behind a structured history — branches explored, decisions made, costs incurred, outcomes observed. As shown in Figure 2, we treat this history as an empirical replay simulator: a grounded model of the part of the discovery space already seen. Inside this simulator, a different exploration policy simply traces a different path through the recorded discovery tree, choosing other branches, another ordering, a different degree of parallelism, or an earlier stopping point. Scoring that path only requires revealing outcomes already stored along it; no rerun of the coding agent or evaluator is needed. One expensive online run therefore funds many cheap evaluations of alternative strategies.

3 Dream-RSI: RSI through Evolving Worlds

As shown in Figure 1, Dream-RSI alternates between online exploration and offline “dreaming” for policy evaluation to improve the exploration policy that allocates discovery computation. For online rollout, the exploration policy directs a fixed discovery agent to generate a tree-structure discovery trace, where each node in the tree is an discovery attempt and is scored by a fixed evaluator. The discovery tree then becomes a replay world: alternative policies can be re-evaluated against stored outcomes. In the offline dreaming phase, a fixed agent iteratively revises the code for the exploration policy, and every revision is evaluated in all stored replay worlds. The best version is then deployed for the next online rollout. Only the policy code changes; the models, evaluator, and execution interfaces stay fixed.

Discovery trees and the shared decision interface.

A discovery tree is rooted at rr, the initial workspace state. Every non-root node vv has exactly one primary parent (root or a previous node), which decides where its attempt begins: the discovery agent resumes the parent’s saved workspace and inherits its accumulated observations as context to generate the attempt in vv. Node vv keeps all previous generation history for it, and its own filesystem snapshot, together with an evaluation score svs_{v}. Scores are generated from a fixed protocol, and larger values are better. We define the root score sr=0s_{r}=0. In both online rollout and offline evaluation, the exploration policy observes a tree 𝒯\mathcal{T}, initially containing only the root, and selects nodes in 𝒯\mathcal{T} to continue exploration. The eligible nodes are A⁡(𝒯)={r}∪{v∈𝒯:v​ is a leaf}A(\mathcal{T})=\{r\}\cup\{v\in\mathcal{T}:v\text{ is a leaf}\}, which contains the root and all leave node in the current tree. We assume there are W≥1W\geq 1 parallel workers, each running one generation–evaluation request at a time (e.g. concurrent API calls). For the current tree 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the exploration policy’s action is a batch C∈A⁡(𝒯,W)C\in A(\mathcal{T};W), where A⁡(𝒯,W)={C⊆A⁡(𝒯):|C|≤W}A(\mathcal{T};W)=\{C\subseteq A(\mathcal{T}):|C|\leq W\} is the feasible batch set. The batch determines both where exploration continues and how many attempts run concurrently. Both the online and offline phase use this decision interface, and differ only in how state transitions after an action: one executes for real, the other replays.

Online rollout.

Let t=1,2,…t=1,2,\ldots index iterations of online rollout, starting from policy π1\pi_{1} and empty history ℋ0=()\mathcal{H}_{0}=(). At iteration tt, the fixed policy πt\pi_{t} guides the discovery agent to generate a new online rollout with access to the completed discovery history ℋt−1\mathcal{H}_{t-1} as context. The history informs exploration but is kept separate from the tree under construction. Let 𝒯tk\mathcal{T}_{t}^{k} be the discovery tree after kk completed rounds at iteration tt, with 𝒯t0={r}\mathcal{T}_{t}^{0}=\{r\}, and allow at most K1K_{1} rounds. At round k<K1k<K_{1}, the policy picks Ctk∈A⁡(𝒯tk,W)C_{t}^{k}\in A(\mathcal{T}_{t}^{k};W) and assigns each v∈Ctkv\in C_{t}^{k} to a worker, which resumes vv’s workspace, generates a candidate, and evaluates it. These attempts run in parallel and each adds one child to its selected parent. Thus, every v∈Ctkv\in C_{t}^{k} is attached with a child, giving 𝒯tk+1\mathcal{T}_{t}^{k+1}. The transition from 𝒯tk\mathcal{T}_{t}^{k} to 𝒯tk+1\mathcal{T}_{t}^{k+1} is stochastic, since the agent may produce different outcomes from the same workspace. For the next round, each newly added node becomes the selectable leaf of its branch, while rr stays selectable for opening new branches. The rollout ends when Ctk=∅C_{t}^{k}=\emptyset or after K1K_{1} completed rounds. After the rollout terminates, its final tree is recorded as 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} and appended to the history, giving ℋt=ℋt−1∪{𝒯t}\mathcal{H}_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\cup\{\mathcal{T}_{t}\}. The method then enters the offline evaluaton phase using ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}.

Offline evaluation.

With ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} fixed, our method constructs and evaluates M≥1M\geq 1 policy versions πt0,…,πtM−1\pi_{t}^{0},\ldots,\pi_{t}^{M-1}, where πt0=πt\pi_{t}^{0}=\pi_{t}. Each version is evaluated on every historical tree 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i}, i=1,…,ti=1,\ldots,t, under budget-control parameters ρ∈ℛ:={0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}\rho\in\mathcal{R}:=\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\}, where ρ\rho controls the policy’s budget preference. The resulting feedback drives the next policy version. We index policy versions by mm, replay worlds by ii, budget preferences by ρ\rho, and decision rounds within one replay by kk. The outer index tt is fixed and omitted below. For each (m,i,ρ)(m,i,\rho), replay starts from 𝒯i,ρm,0={r}\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,0}=\{r\}, where 𝒯i,ρm,k⊆𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{i} is the subtree revealed after kk completed rounds. The recorded tree 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} never changes; only the observed portion grows. At round k<K2k<K_{2}, the current policy πtm\pi_{t}^{m}, conditioned on ρ\rho, selects Ci,ρm,k∈A⁡(𝒯i,ρm,k,W)C_{i,\rho}^{m,k}\in A(\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k};W) from the revealed observations. Unlike online execution, offline replay returns recorded children of the selected nodes deterministically rather than generating new candidates. Thus, 𝒯i,ρm,k+1=𝒯i,ρm,k∪⋃v∈Ci,ρm,kChild⁡(v,𝒯i,𝒯i,ρm,k)\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k+1}=\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k}\cup\bigcup_{v\in C_{i,\rho}^{m,k}}\operatorname{Child}(v;\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k}), where Child⁡(v,𝒯i,𝒯i,ρm,k)\operatorname{Child}(v;\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k}) contains unobserved children of vv in 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} given the current revealed subtree. For v≠rv\neq r, it is vv’s unique recorded child, if one exists. For v=rv=r, it is the earliest-created child of rr outside 𝒯i,ρm,k\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k}, opening one previously unrevealed branch. In either case, Child⁡(v,𝒯i,𝒯i,ρm,k)=∅\operatorname{Child}(v;\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k})=\emptyset when no unobserved continuation remains. Newly revealed nodes expose their stored observations before the policy makes its next decision. Replay permits at most K2K_{2} rounds, counting each nonempty batch as one completed round, and stops when Ci,ρm,k=∅C_{i,\rho}^{m,k}=\emptyset, after K2K_{2} completed rounds, or when 𝒯i,ρm,k=𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k}=\mathcal{T}_{i}. Let ki,ρm,⋆∈{0,…,K2}k_{i,\rho}^{m,\star}\in\{0,\ldots,K_{2}\} denote the number of completed rounds at termination. The final observed subtree is 𝒯i,ρm,ki,ρm,⋆⊆𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k_{i,\rho}^{m,\star}}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{i}. Replay thus measures how far a policy pursues each branch, how it groups attempts into parallel batches, and when it opens a new branch or stops. These choices vary across policies and budget preferences, but every branch is traversed in its recorded parent–child order, and no outcome outside 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} is produced.

Replay objective.

The replay objective balances discovery quality and generation cost across budget preferences while also favoring parallel execution. For each replay world 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} used for evaluation, define Bi:=|𝒯i|−1>0B_{i}:=|\mathcal{T}_{i}|-1>0 and Si:=maxv∈𝒯i∖{r}⁡sv>0S_{i}:=\max_{v\in\mathcal{T}_{i}\setminus\{r\}}s_{v}>0, the total number of evaluated non-root nodes and the best recorded score, respectively. For each ρ∈ℛ\rho\in\mathcal{R}, let ni,ρm:=|𝒯i,ρm,ki,ρm,⋆|−1n_{i,\rho}^{m}:=|\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k_{i,\rho}^{m,\star}}|-1 be the number of discovery-agent calls represented by the replay. Let si,ρms_{i,\rho}^{m} be the best score among the revealed non-root nodes, i.e., si,ρm:=maxv∈𝒯i,ρm,ki,ρm,⋆∖{r}⁡svs_{i,\rho}^{m}:=\max_{v\in\mathcal{T}_{i,\rho}^{m,k_{i,\rho}^{m,\star}}\setminus\{r\}}s_{v} when ni,ρm>0n_{i,\rho}^{m}>0, and set si,ρm:=0s_{i,\rho}^{m}:=0 otherwise. We normalize the attained quality as ai,ρm:=clip⁡(si,ρm/Si,0,1)a_{i,\rho}^{m}:=\operatorname{clip}(s_{i,\rho}^{m}/S_{i},0,1). The budget sweep produces the quality–cost points {(ni,ρm,ai,ρm):ρ∈ℛ}\{(n_{i,\rho}^{m},a_{i,\rho}^{m}):\rho\in\mathcal{R}\}. A point is dominated if another point uses no more calls and attains no lower quality, with at least one strict improvement. Let (n¯i,jm,a¯i,jm)j=1Lim(\bar{n}_{i,j}^{m},\bar{a}_{i,j}^{m})_{j=1}^{L_{i}^{m}} be the distinct nondominated points ordered by increasing call count, and set a¯i,0m:=0\bar{a}_{i,0}^{m}:=0. The replay score is

Vim:=1Bi​∑j=1Lim(a¯i,jm−a¯i,j−1m)​(Bi−n¯i,jm)⏟normalized hypervolume−λ​1|ℛ|​∑ρ∈ℛni,ρm>0ki,ρm,⋆ni,ρm⏟parallelism penalty.V_{i}^{m}:=\underbrace{\frac{1}{B_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{i}^{m}}\bigl(\bar{a}_{i,j}^{m}-\bar{a}_{i,j-1}^{m}\bigr)\bigl(B_{i}-\bar{n}_{i,j}^{m}\bigr)}_{\text{normalized hypervolume}}-\lambda\underbrace{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\in\mathcal{R}\\ n_{i,\rho}^{m}>0\end{subarray}}\frac{k_{i,\rho}^{m,\star}}{n_{i,\rho}^{m}}}_{\text{parallelism penalty}}. (1)

Here, λ\lambda controls the strength of the parallelism penalty. The first term measures the normalized area dominated by the quality–cost Pareto frontier, rewarding policies that attain higher quality with fewer discovery-agent calls. The second term measures the average number of completed sequential rounds per call across the budget sweep, thereby favoring policies that execute more calls in parallel; replays with zero calls contribute zero to this term.

Policy improvement and selection.

A policy version πtm\pi_{t}^{m} is evaluated by its average replay score over ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}, denoted by Vm=1t​∑i=1tVimV^{m}=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}V_{i}^{m}. The offline phase starts πt0=πt\pi_{t}^{0}=\pi_{t}. At each step m=0,…,M−2m=0,\ldots,M-2, a policy-development agent inspects the replay trajectories and scores of πtm\pi_{t}^{m}, along with feedback from earlier revisions, to identify successful decisions and recurring failures. It then rewrites the executable policy code into πtm+1\pi_{t}^{m+1}, which is evaluated on the same tt replay worlds. The next online policy is the best-scoring candidate, πt+1=πtm⋆\pi_{t+1}=\pi_{t}^{m^{\star}} with m⋆∈arg​maxm∈{0,⋯,M−1}⁡Vmm^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{m\in\{0,\cdots,M-1\}}V^{m}. Since the current rollout policy πt=πt0\pi_{t}=\pi_{t}^{0} is included among the candidates, Vm⋆≥V0V^{m^{\star}}\geq V^{0}, so πt+1\pi_{t+1} is never worse than πt\pi_{t} on the average replay score over HtH_{t}.

4 Experiments

We evaluate Dream-RSI on algorithm engineering, kernel optimization, mathematical optimization, and harness optimization. We primarily use Gemini-3.1-Pro for scientific discovery experiments, with additional Lasso experiments using Gemini-3.7-Flash to assess applicability across backbones. For harness optimization, we use Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code. On the scientific discovery tasks, our main controlled baseline is Recursive Fixed Exploration. Both methods use identical discovery agents, evaluators, initialization, per-round budget limits, and the same hand-designed starting policy. From the second round onward, Recursive Fixed Exploration keeps its policy fixed, while Dream-RSI updates it through replay-based dreaming over accumulated discovery history. For harness optimization, we focus on end-to-end performance and omit the fixed-policy comparison due to its substantial cost: an additional full search is estimated to cost over $100,000. We measure discovery cost as the cumulative number of discovery-agent calls.

4.1 Kernel Engineering

The goal of kernel engineering is to discover high-performance kernel implementations while preserving numerical correctness. We use four representative KernelBench tasks (Ouyang et al., 2025): VGG16, LayerNorm, ConvDiv, and ConvMax. Candidates are scored by execution performance, measured as inverse runtime (1/ms1/\mathrm{ms}), subject to correctness checks against the reference implementation. With Gemini-3.1 Pro as the coding agent, we compare Dream-RSI against Recursive Fixed Exploration under an identical evaluation protocol and initialization, and against the strong PaceEvolve baseline (Yan et al., 2026b), whose maximum discovery time we cap at two days for fairness.

Results.

Figure 3 shows discovery trajectories as the number of generations increases. On VGG16 and LayerNorm, Dream-RSI matches final performance with 2.43×2.43\times and 1.79×1.79\times fewer generations. On ConvDiv and ConvMax, under comparable budgets, it achieves 2.09×2.09\times and 1.44×1.44\times higher performance. Adapting the exploration policy across recursive rounds thus improves both the efficiency and the effectiveness of long-horizon discovery, and Dream-RSI surpasses PACEvolve in kernel performance (Detailed PACEvolve scaling curves are provided in Appendix C.). Appendix E.2 gives the discovered ConvDiv kernel. Rather than optimizing convolution in isolation, it restructures the operator chain around downstream pooling and reduction. Adjacent convolution outputs are max-pooled immediately, while width pooling and subsequent reductions run directly on register-resident values, avoiding materialization of convolution and pooled feature maps. Linear operations, such as scaling, averaging, and bias accumulation, are deferred to a lightweight final reduction.

4.2 Mathematics Optimization

We further evaluate Dream-RSI on three mathematical discovery tasks spanning discrete combinatorial optimization, geometric optimization, and functional optimization: the Sum–Difference Problem, Circle Packing, and Autocorrelation Inequalities. Formal definitions of the three tasks are provided in Appendix B.3. We use Gemini-3.1 Pro via the Gemini CLI as the discovery agent for both methods for 10 rounds. For each task, the agent iteratively proposes and evaluates candidate constructions or optimization procedures according to the task-specific objective.

Results.

Table 1 summarizes the results. Dream-RSI achieves a Sum–Difference score of 1.1454271.145427, outperforming SimpleTES and Recursive Fixed Exploration. On Circle Packing, it reaches 2.6359832.635983, matching the strongest reported result among the compared methods. For Autocorrelation, Dream-RSI obtains 1.4563751.456375, remaining competitive with existing discovery systems.

4.3 Algorithm Engineering

In this task, we consider Lasso Regularization Path as our algorithm-engineering task, a fundamental computational primitive in high-dimensional statistics that is widely used in model selection and cross-validation across domains such as genomics and finance. We follow the benchmark setting of SimpleTES (Ye et al., 2026), where the goal is to discover efficient implementations of the complete Lasso regularization path while preserving numerical correctness. During discovery, we use the same 17 synthetic instances as SimpleTES, which cover diverse problem regimes in terms of dimensionality, sparsity, feature correlation, and active-set structure. To evaluate whether the discovered algorithms generalize beyond the search distribution, we additionally evaluate them on six held-out downstream datasets spanning biological and non-biological domains. We compare against standard Lasso solvers sklearn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) and glmnet (Friedman et al., 2010), as well as SimpleTES (Ye et al., 2026). We run both controlled baseline and Dream-RSI for 5 rounds.

Main Results.

Figure 4(a) summarizes the Lasso discovery results. Across both discovery-agent backbones, Dream-RSI achieves a better downstream quality–compute trade-off than Recursive Fixed Exploration. With Gemini-3.1 Pro, it reduces the average runtime across the six held-out datasets from 3587.1 ms to 2931.0 ms while using only 317 discovery-agent calls, compared with 550 calls for fixed exploration. With Gemini-3.7-Flash, Dream-RSI further reduces the average runtime from 2516.7 ms to 2350.6 ms using 1879 calls instead of 3200. Despite using substantially less discovery compute, the resulting solvers also outperform the standard sklearn and glmnet implementations on all six held-out datasets. Relative to SimpleTES’s reported 51,200 generations, our Pro and Flash runs use approximately 162×\times and 27×\times fewer discovery-agent calls, respectively, with lower average downstream runtime, although these comparisons use different model backbones. For 3.1 Pro, the average improvement over fixed exploration is driven by RCV1, despite slower runtimes on the other five datasets. For 3.7 Flash, runtime improves on five of the six datasets.

Recursive Discovery Dynamics.

Figure 4(b) shows the trajectory of downstream performance across recursive discovery rounds against cumulative discovery compute. By design, both methods behave identically in the first round. Afterward, Recursive Fixed Exploration keeps a static exploration policy, while Dream-RSI iteratively refines and redeploys its policy by dreaming over accumulated discovery history. By the final round, Dream-RSI achieves lower average downstream runtime with fewer discovery-agent calls than Recursive Fixed Exploration on both backbones. We further examine the discovered solver, whose implementation appears in Appendix E.1. Unlike SimpleTES, which switches between LARS and coordinate descent by problem dimension, the discovered solver makes the active-set optimization itself adaptive. It pairs strong-rule screening with Cauchy–Schwarz KKT pruning, computing exact gradients only when necessary and falling back to a full refresh once pruning loses effectiveness.

4.4 Harness Optimization

We further evaluate Dream-RSI on the harness optimization task, where the goal is to improve the program surrounding a fixed language model, including how information is stored, retrieved, and presented during agent execution. We follow the setting of Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) and initialize the discovery from Terminus-Kira as the seed harness. Each discovered harness is evaluated on the full Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) suite of 89 tasks, with two independent runs per task. We use Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code as both the discovery agent and the policy-development agent, while harness evaluation is also performed with Claude Opus 4.8. We reproduce Meta-Harness following its original search protocol, using Opus 4.8 for both search and evaluation.

Results.

Figure 5 shows that Dream-RSI improves the harness throughout the discovery process, increasing the full-suite score from 0.7247 to 0.8090. The discovered harness also outperforms Claude Code (0.75) and Meta-Harness (0.79) under the same evaluation setting.

5 Further Analysis

Analysis of Replay World Accumulation

We study the effect of accumulating replay worlds across recursive rounds. Table 2 shows that Dream-RSI achieves a performance of 1.90 using the full discovery history, compared with 1.59 when replay is restricted to the current round. Accumulating replay worlds may help learn a more general exploration policy and avoid overly conservative exploration associated with fitting to a single world.

Analysis of Historical Inductive Biases in Long-Horizon Discovery

We further investigate how the nature of the historical inductive bias affects long-horizon discovery. A natural alternative for utilizing history is to abstract prior trajectories into high-level directional insights, which are directly injected into the prompt as explicit semantic guidance for subsequent rounds. To evaluate the efficacy of this prompt-level semantic guidance, we apply it to both Recursive Fixed Exploration and Dream-RSI. As illustrated in Figure 6, explicit directional guidance yields lower final performance for both methods on ConvDiv. This suggests that such guidance may constrain exploration.

Analysis of Evolution of Exploration Behavior

Figure 7 illustrates how the learned exploration policy evolves across recursive rounds on ConvDiv. The exploration policy exhibits an adaptive pattern: as performance improves, it initially conserves discovery compute (e.g., reducing the number of evaluated attempts from 110 to 50). When progress subsequently plateaus, it increases exploration effort again, coinciding with further performance gains.

6 Related Work

AI-Driven Scientific and Algorithmic Discovery.

LLM-based discovery systems iteratively generate, evaluate, and refine candidate solutions using prior artifacts and feedback, as in AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025), CodeEvolve (Assumpção et al., 2025), ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), PACEvolve (Yan et al., 2026b), DeltaEvolve (Jiang et al., 2026) and MLEvolve Du et al. (2026). More recent work emphasizes the importance of exploration itself: SkyDiscover provides adaptive discovery infrastructure (Liu et al., 2026b), SwarmResearch dynamically orchestrates multiple search branches (Virk et al., 2026), and EvoX (Liu et al., 2026a) explicitly optimizes search strategies rather than only candidate solutions. This shift makes exploration a meta-level optimization problem, but useful supervision for exploration strategies is expensive and delayed because their quality often becomes apparent only after long discovery rollouts.

Self-Evolving Agents.

A broader line of work studies agents that improve their own components during interaction. Prior methods evolve model weights (Huang et al., 2026c; Huang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a), agent harnesses (Lee et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b), contexts (Zhang et al., 2026d), skills (Zhang et al., 2026a; Ouyang et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026b), model behavior through test-time learning (Wang et al., 2025; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026a), rubrics (Xiong et al., 2026), environments (Huang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026b) and other applications (Dai et al., 2026). Most operate at the object level, improving components used for task execution or reasoning. Recent work has begun to optimize meta-level mechanisms, including search strategies and self-improvement procedures (Liu et al., 2026a; Yan et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Kim et al., 2026). However, such meta-level strategies are difficult to improve because their quality is often revealed only after costly long-horizon rollouts. Dream-RSI turns accumulated discovery history into replay simulators for off-policy evaluation and refinement of exploration policies, then redeploys the selected policy for new online discovery, closing a recursive self-improvement loop.

Memory, History, and Experience Reuse.

Prior work reuses agent experience as search history, context, memory, reusable skills, or training signals. DeltaEvolve structures evolutionary history through semantic deltas (Jiang et al., 2026); SwarmResearch and MLEvolve use cross-branch or retrospective information to guide subsequent search (Virk et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026); and other work improves how agents access and retain experience through evolving contexts, broader harness state, libraries, or skills (Zhang et al., 2026d; Lee et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026a). We take a different view: rather than using exploration history only as context or memory for the next decision, we organize it as a replay simulator in which many alternative exploration controllers can be evaluated cheaply. This turns previously collected discovery experience into reusable feedback for meta-level optimization, alleviating the scarcity and high cost of training signals.

7 Conclusion

We presented Dream-RSI, a framework for the recursive self-improvement of exploration policies in long-horizon discovery. The central idea in Dream-RSI is to convert accumulated discovery history from static context into an active, replayable simulator, directly targeting the core bottleneck of meta-optimization: delayed and expensive feedback. By "dreaming" within replay simulators constructed from historical discovery trees, Dream-RSI evaluates candidate exploration policies rapidly and at negligible execution cost. Improved policies are then redeployed online, driving further discovery and expanding the simulator pool — closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Our experiments demonstrate competitive discovery quality across diverse domains and improved discovery-agent-call efficiency in several settings.

Appendix A AI Use Statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools as the API in the experiments, as described in the paper: we use Gemini 3.1 Pro in the Section 4.1,4.2,4.3, Gemini 3.7 Flash in Section 4.3 and Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code in the Section4.4. Additionally, we used Gemini 3.8 Flash for writing and grammar correction. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Appendix B Detailed Experimental Settings

B.1 Evaluation Environments

Lasso regularization-path discovery.

We evaluate candidate solvers in a KVM virtual machine with an AMD EPYC 7B12 processor, 8 vCPUs, and 32 GB RAM, running Debian-based Linux. The evaluation protocol follows Ye et al. (2026).

GPU kernel engineering.

We evaluate candidate kernels on an NVIDIA L40S GPU. Numerical correctness is checked against the reference PyTorch implementation following the official KernelBench protocol (Ouyang et al., 2025).

Mathematical optimization.

We use the same hardware environment as for Lasso regularization-path discovery.

Harness optimization.

We evaluate candidate harnesses on a CPU server with 96 physical cores (192 logical CPUs) and 708 GiB RAM, using Docker to provide isolated task execution environments.

B.2 Discovery Configuration

Table 3 summarizes the discovery configurations. Each offline phase evaluates the current policy and three newly generated policy versions (M=4M=4). The parenthesized budget decomposition specifies the maximum number of branches and attempts per branch, including the initial attempt. These budgets are upper limits; actual discovery-agent calls depend on the policy’s allocation and stopping decisions.

B.3 Detailed Task Description

Appendix C Results of PACEvolve (Yan et al., 2026b) on KernelBench

We present the detailed discovery process of PACEvolve (Yan et al., 2026b) on KernelBench in Figure 8. For a controlled comparison, we allow PACEvolve a 48-hour wall-clock budget on each task and report its best-so-far performance throughout the search.

Appendix D Prompts

For reproducibility, we provide the prompts used for online exploration and replay-based exploration-policy improvement. Variables enclosed by dollar signs or braces are instantiated by the runtime system before execution.

D.1 Exploration Prompt

The following prompt is used to guide the discovery agent during online exploration. It requires the agent to inspect the complete available discovery history before proposing a new solution, explicitly reason about both successful and failed attempts, and avoid repeatedly exploiting a locally saturated direction.

D.2 Replay-Based Policy Improvement Prompt

The following prompt is used by the controller-development agent during historical replay. The agent modifies the exploration policy using feedback obtained from replay over previously collected discovery trajectories while remaining restricted to prefix-observable information.

Appendix E Discovered Programs

E.1 Lasso Regularization Path

We provide the complete implementation of the Lasso-path solver discovered by Dream-RSI. As discussed in Section 4.3, the solver combines strong-rule screening with adaptive Cauchy–Schwarz KKT pruning, disjoint active-set bookkeeping, lazy Gram-matrix construction, and hardware-aware optimizations.
